title: Blanket Implementations

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A generic `impl` can grant a trait to all types satisfying a bound. Blanket implementations are powerful because they shape which future implementations remain legal under coherence rules.

A blanket implementation defines one rule for every type satisfying a bound. In the example, any sized `T` that implements `Display` also receives `Named`, whose `name()` delegates to `to_string()`. This avoids writing essentially the same implementation for each printable type. The benefit is broad, but so is the commitment: every current and future `Display` type covered by the rule gets that behavior.

Trace a call on an integer and one on a custom struct with `Display`. Both resolve to the same generic implementation, specialized for their concrete type. A type without `Display` has no `Named` implementation from this blanket rule, so a caller demanding `Named` cannot use it. The implicit `Sized` bound on `T` also leaves out `str` itself, unless the `impl` adds `?Sized`. This is a compile-time capability relationship, not a runtime registry. The code does not inspect the type's name or perform a dynamic check.

Blanket implementations interact with coherence. If your crate already grants `Named` to all `Display` types, a more specific `Named` implementation for one overlapping `Display` type conflicts on stable Rust. Also, the orphan rules limit which trait/type combinations your crate may implement. Before publishing a broad blanket `impl`, ask whether future special cases should behave differently. Try adding an overlapping implementation and read the compiler error. Sometimes a newtype wrapper or a narrower bound gives users more room to customize behavior later.

As a design exercise, imagine a type whose `Display` format changes over time. Would the generated name remain appropriate? A blanket rule is strongest when the mapping from the bound to the new behavior is stable for all covered types.
